title_original: 32 Inspiring Photobooks to Give this Holiday Season
excerpt_original: Iconic monographs. Must-read essay books. Exclusive limited-editions. Here is the ultimate guide to the best photobooks for everyone on your gift list.

Debut Photobooks
Elle Pérez: Devotions

Love, heartache, pleasure, pain—Elle Pérez has emerged as a defining voice of their generation, making disarmingly intimate images that portray states of emotional intensity and physical transformation. Pérez started out as a teenager photographing underground spaces around New York, making a tender and vivid record of unalloyed freedom. Since then, their work has ranged from striking portraits to crystalline landscapes, and multimedia collages that incorporate influences across art and literature. Devotions is the first monograph focused on their work, collecting the artist’s most influential works from 2009 to the present—alongside the ephemera, notes, and research that inform their singular vision.
Myriam Boulos: What’s Ours

In her searing, diaristic portrait of a city and society in revolution, Myriam Boulos creates an intimate portrait of youth, queerness, and protest. What’s Ours , her debut monograph, brings together over a decade of images, casting a determined eye on the revolution that began in Lebanon in 2019 with protests against government corruption and austerity—culminating with the aftermath of the devastating Beirut port explosion of August 2020. Photographing her friends and family with energy and intimacy, “Boulos’s lens inspires and entices her subjects,” writes Mona Eltahawy in an accompanying essay. “They know they have an ally, a secret sharer in their intimacy who then shares them with the rest of us.”
Collect a limited-edition book and print set of Myriam Boulos: What’s Ours featuring a signed print by the artist and a copy of the book.
David Alekhuogie: A Reprise

In A Reprise , David Alekhuogie remixes Walker Evans’s photographs of African art, provoking timely questions about authorship and authenticity. In 1935, Walker Evans photographed hundreds of African sculptures for the exhibition African Negro Art at the Museum of Modern Art, New York. Alekhuogie investigates Evans’s photographs, provocatively remixing them into vibrant collages, and confronting the legacy of authorship behind Western perceptions of African art. Drawing upon the musical concept of the reprise—a performance of repetition—Alekhuogie’s first monograph stakes a claim to restorative ideas around Black antiquity by questioning our relationship to what we consider fake or original, art or archive.
Coreen Simpson: A Monograph

Coreen Simpson—photographer, writer, jeweler— has done it all . Coreen Simpson: A Monograph is a comprehensive survey of a singular, creative force who interweaves photography, design, and explorations of identity. Working for publications such as Essence , Unique New York , and The Village Voice , from the late 1970s onward, Simpson covered New York’s art and fashion scenes, producing portraits of Black artists, literary figures, and celebrities. Her iconic jewelry, the Black Cameo, has been worn by everyone from the model Iman to civil-rights leader Rosa Parks. This long-awaited volume, Simpson’s first, features her celebrated B-Boys series—portraits of young people coming of age during the early years of hip-hop—as well as her experiments with collage and other formal interventions.
Collect a limited-edition print from Coreen Simpson: A Monograph .
Words & Pictures
Aperture Magazine Subscription

The source for photography and ideas since 1952, Aperture features immersive portfolios, in-depth writing, and must-read interviews with today’s leading artists. Each issue is organized around a compelling theme and features work ranging from the historical to contemporary. Numerous luminaries have guest-edited editions—including Deana Lawson, Alec Soth, Tilda Swinton, Hiroshi Sugimoto, Wolfgang Tillmans, and more—making the magazine essential reading for anyone interested in photography and contemporary culture.
Through December 31, gift Aperture and save 40% off the cover price.
Josef Koudelka: Diaries

Diaries is a rare glimpse into the mind and artistic process of one of the world’s greatest photographers. Distilled from sixty‑nine journals kept by Josef Koudelka over the course of fifty‑plus years, Diaries offers a look inside the mind and artistic process of the iconoclastic Czech photographer renowned for a life in exile and legendary projects on the Roma, the 1968 Soviet-led invasion of Czechoslovakia, and the devastating impact humans have made on the landscape. Facsimile pages from the diaries, along with images by the photographer, including self‑portraits, lend the volume an immediacy and authenticity.
Collect a special bundle of Diaries with the artist’s definitive biography, Next.
The Photography Workshop Book Series

In the Photography Workshop Series, Aperture works with the world’s top photographers to distill their creative approaches, teachings, and insights, offering a workshop experience in a book. Whether it’s Catherine Opie on developing your artistic voice in collaboration with others, Vik Muniz on seeing the familiar in new and surprising ways, or Dawoud Bey on photographing people and communities, these books offer inspiration to photographers at all levels who wish to improve their work, as well as readers interested in deepening their understanding of the art of photography.
Race Stories: Essays on the Power of Images

links.text: Race Stories: Essays on the Power of Images

blocks.text: Race Stories brings together a collection of award-winning short essays by the late cultural historian Maurice Berger that explore the intersections of photography, race, and visual culture. Edited by Marvin Heiferman, Race Stories features seventy-one essays paired with 189 photographs, examining the transformational role photography plays in shaping ideas and attitudes about race and how photographic images have been instrumental in both perpetuating and combating racial stereotypes. This volume is the first title in Aperture’s Vision & Justice Book Series—created and coedited by Drs. Sarah Lewis, Leigh Raiford, and Deborah Willis—which reexamines and redresses historical narratives of photography, race, and justice.
Photo No-Nos: Meditations on What Not to Photograph

links.text: Photo No-Nos: Meditations on What Not to Photograph

blocks.text: What’s a “photo no-no”? Photographers often have unwritten lists of subjects they tell themselves not to shoot—things that are cliché, exploitative, derivative, or sometimes even arbitrary. Edited by Jason Fulford, this volume brings together ideas, stories, and anecdotes from over two hundred photographers and photography professionals. Not a strict guide but a series of meditations on pictures, Photo No-Nos covers a wide range of topics, from sunsets and roses to issues of colonialism, stereotypes, and social responsibility—offering a timely, thoughtful, and often amusing resource on what photographers consider to be off-limits, and how they have contended with their own self-imposed rules without being paralyzed by them.
Aperture Ideas Series

The Aperture Ideas series highlights the sharpest critical and creative minds exploring key concepts in photography. At the Limits of the Gaze collects the writings of Takuma Nakahira in English for the first time, bringing together the Japanese photographer’s boundary-pushing essays that challenge the expressive limits of photography. In Strange Hours: Photography, Memory, and the Lives of Artists , Rebecca Bengal considers the photographers who have defined our relationship to the medium. Continually questioning given forms of identity since the 1970s, Sunil Gupta illuminates the essential connections between queer migration and self-discovery in We Were Here: Sexuality, Photography, and Cultural Difference .
Aperture Legends
Nan Goldin: The Ballad of Sexual Dependency

links.text: Nan Goldin: The Ballad of Sexual Dependency

blocks.text: First published by Aperture in 1986, Nan Goldin’s The Ballad of Sexual Dependency has had a profound influence on photography and visual culture around the world for the past forty years and counting. Goldin’s visceral chronicle of her friends, family, and lovers in the 1970s and ’80s captured a world teeming with life while challenging censorship, disrupting gender stereotypes, and bringing crucial visibility to the AIDS crisis. As Goldin reflects in an afterword in 2021: “I took the pictures in this book so that nostalgia could never color my past. I wanted to make a record of my life that nobody could revise.”
Robert Frank: The Americans

In the nearly seven decades since its publication in the 1950s, Robert Frank’s The Americans has become one of the most influential and enduring works of American photography. Through eighty-three photographs taken across the country, Frank unveiled an America that had gone previously unacknowledged—confronting its people with an underbelly of racial inequality, corruption, injustice, and the stark reality of the American dream. In 2024, to mark the centennial of Frank’s birth, Aperture reissued The Americans , alongside a special centennial edition with a slipcase and featuring a booklet showcasing Frank’s early films.
Josef Koudelka: Invasion Prague 68

When Soviet-led troops invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968, Josef Koudelka was one of the first on the scene. An acclaimed theater photographer, Koudelka knew nothing about photojournalism, but that would soon change. In the turmoil, he took a series of photographs purely for himself, which were miraculously smuggled out of the country. A year after they reached New York, Magnum Photos distributed and credited the photos to an unknown Czech photographer. Sixteen years would pass before Koudelka could safely acknowledge authorship. This hardcover edition of Invasion Prague 68 reinstates the vitality and prescience of Koudelka’s work in capturing defiance in the face of suppression.
Joel Meyerowitz: Cape Light

Joel Meyerowitz’s series of serene and contemplative color photographs taken on Cape Cod, Massachusetts, quickly became a timeless classic after the first publication of Cape Light in 1978. Everyday scenes—an approaching storm, a grocery store at dusk, the view through a bedroom window—are transformed by the stunning light of Cape Cod and the luminous vision of the photographer, and through his eyes small-town life on the cape is imbued with a powerful and captivating beauty. This fiftieth anniversary reissue features the iconic images of the original edition, newly remastered and printed as never before.
An-My Lê: Small Wars

For the past three decades, An-My Lê has used photography to examine her personal history and the legacies of US military power, probing the tension between experience and storytelling. First published by Aperture in 2005, this twentieth anniversary reissue brings together three of Lê’s interconnected series— Viêt Nam , Small Wars , and 29 Palms —presenting a complexly layered exploration of the issues surrounding landscape, memory, and the representation of violence and war. A new afterword by Ocean Vuong considers how this work resonates twenty years on.
Zanele Muholi: Somnyama Ngonyama, Hail the Dark Lioness, Volume I

links.text: Zanele Muholi: Somnyama Ngonyama, Hail the Dark Lioness, Volume I

blocks.text: In the evocative self-portraits collected in Somnyama Ngonyama, Hail the Dark Lioness (2018), Zanele Muholi explores and expands upon notions of Blackness and the myriad possibilities of the self. Drawing on different materials or found objects referencing their environment, a specific event, or lived experience, Muholi boldly explores their own image and innate possibilities as a Black person in global society, and speaks emphatically in response to contemporary and historical racisms. In 2024, Aperture released the highly anticipated follow-up to this work in Somnyama Ngonyama, Hail the Dark Lioness, Volume II .

blocks.text: Contemporary Classics
Kwame Brathwaite: Black Is Beautiful

Kwame Brathwaite’s photographs from the 1950s and ’60s transformed how we define Blackness. Using his photography to popularize the Black Is Beautiful movement, Brathwaite challenged mainstream beauty standards. Born in Brooklyn and part of the second-wave Harlem Renaissance, Brathwaite and his brother Elombe Brath were responsible for creating the African Jazz-Arts Society and Studios (AJASS) and the Grandassa Models. Black Is Beautiful is the defining monograph dedicated to Brathwaite’s influential and remarkable career.
Ishiuchi Miyako: Traces

Ishiuchi Miyako is one of Japan’s foremost photographers, and since beginning her career in the 1970s, she has lead the way for female practitioners in a traditionally male-dominated scene. Through subjects as diverse as old apartment blocks, human scars, kimono fabrics, and personal belongings of the deceased, Ishiuchi manifests the invisible, capturing time, atmosphere, and memory. Traces charts the course of her practice over fifty years and identifies themes that resurface throughout her work, including her relationship with place, the passage of time, and the bodies and possessions of people, always with an emphasis on materiality and ephemerality.
Tina Barney: Fashion

Renowned for her large-format tableaux of affluent families in the United States and Europe, Tina Barney is a keen observer of style and its coded web of meanings. Blending personal history, family albums, and work made on assignment, Fashion is the first monograph to trace the role of sartorial expression across the celebrated portraitist’s long career—offering a fresh take on a classic American photographer.
Sophie Rivera: Double Exposures

Double Exposures is the first bilingual monograph dedicated to Sophie Rivera, a trailblazing artist at the center of feminist engagement and contemporary photography in the US. Renowned for her portraits of everyday Puerto Ricans taken in her home studio in Upper Manhattan, Rivera began her career in the 1970s, becoming part of a coalition of artists who sought to counter negative depictions of Latinos in US popular culture. These portraits, as well as her street photographs, abstract cityscapes, and experimental self-portraits bolstered Rivera’s standing as a leading artist who engaged with feminist and political consciousness throughout her life and work.
Wendy Red Star: Delegation

In her dynamic photographs, Wendy Red Star recasts historical narratives with wit, candor, and a feminist, Indigenous perspective. Delegation is the first comprehensive monograph by Red Star (Apsáalooke/Crow), centering Native American life and material culture through the artist’s imaginative self-portraiture, vivid collages, archival interventions, and site-specific installations. Whether referencing nineteenth-century Crow leaders or 1980s pulp fiction, museum collections or family pictures, she constantly questions the role of the photographer in shaping Indigenous representation.
Collect a limited-edition print from Wendy Red Star: Delegation .
Hal Fischer: Seminal Works

In the late 1970s, as gay men in San Francisco experienced a new sense of freedom following the Stonewall Uprising, Hal Fischer made Gay Semiotics , a photo-text project that categorized denizens of the Castro and Haight-Ashbury neighborhoods by social type such as the “jock” or the “hippie.” The series became an influential record of a libertine era before AIDS, the rise of internet dating apps, and tech industry–accelerated gentrification transformed queer life forever. Seminal Works includes Gay Semiotics together with Fischer’s rarely seen early photography.
Collect a limited-edition print from Hal Fischer: Seminal Works .
Justine Kurland: Girl Pictures

The North American frontier is an enduring symbol of romance, rebellion, escape, and freedom. At the same time, it’s a profoundly masculine myth: cowboys, outlaws, Beat poets. Justine Kurland, known for her idyllic images of American landscapes and their fringe communities, sought to reclaim this space with her now iconic series Girl Pictures . Made between 1997 and 2002, Kurland’s photographs stage scenes of teenage girls as imagined runaways, offering a radical vision of community and feminism.
Collect a limited-edition book and print set Justine Kurland: Girl Pictures featuring a signed print by the artist and a copy of the book.
I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now

links.text: I’m So Happy You Are Here: Japanese Women Photographers from the 1950s to Now

blocks.text: I’m So Happy You Are Here is a celebratory counternarrative to what we know of Japanese photography today. This restorative history presents a wide range of photographic approaches brought to bear on the lived experiences of women in Japanese society. The volume and accompanying traveling exhibition (on view through January 2027 in New York at the International Center of Photography ) showcases the work of twenty-five artists whose voices and practices have shaped the medium’s landscape across seven decades, alongside a range of insightful essays and interviews from leading curators and historians.
Aperture Kids
Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade

links.text: Between the Balloons: My Thanksgiving Parade

blocks.text: Between the Balloons invites readers—young and young at heart—into a world bursting with possibility. Celebrating the 100th anniversary of the famed Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, Between the Balloons transforms familiar sights into extraordinary adventures. Larger-than-life balloon characters, marching bands, and delightful surprises fill every page of this playful blend of photography and illustration. Featuring photographs by E.A. KAHANE, illustrations by New Yorker cartoonist Tom Toro, and a story by Doro Globus, the book reveals the wonder of imagination and where it might take you.
This Equals That

In This Equals That , Jason Fulford and Tamara Shopsin take young viewers on a whimsical journey while teaching associative thinking and visual language. Through a simple narrative and a rhythmic sequence of photographs, the book generates multiple meanings, making the experience of reading the book interactive—readers ask questions and come up with their own answers, drawing on the reader’s imagination.
Go Photo!

Go Photo! Fun Things to Do with a Camera features twenty-three hands-on, creative activities to engage kids in the fun and wonder of photography. Indoors or outdoors, from a half hour to a whole day, alone or with friends, each activity is accessible, playful, and inspiring. From making flip-books to neighborhood maps to pinhole cameras, each project includes illustrated instructions and tips that will guide and motivate young imaginations.
Exclusive Editions
Lee Friedlander: Life Still, Poster and Book Set

links.text: Lee Friedlander: Life Still, Poster and Book Set

blocks.text: For over seventy years, Lee Friedlander has been one of photography’s most celebrated figures. His keen ability to capture the intersections of public and private space, with wit and formal complexity, has taught us to see a vast collective unconscious—revealing the dreams, desires, and delusions hidden in the markers of the everyday world. Life Still , his first collaboration with Aperture, captures the irony and complexity of American life, past and present. This exclusive collectors’ set features a signed and numbered limited-edition poster accompanied by a copy of the book .
Alex Webb: Walking Blues, Deluxe Edition and Print

links.text: Alex Webb: Walking Blues, Deluxe Edition and Print

blocks.text: For Walking Blues , acclaimed street photographer Alex Webb traversed some forty cities across the US, documenting moments of connection between communities with his signature eye for bold color and rhythm. Inspired by the lift and pull of the blues, a quintessential American musical form, Webb’s photographs express the improvisation of chance encounters. The culmination of more than a decade of intuitive, open-minded exploration, Webb’s latest book is a vivid chronicle of urban life today. This special edition of Walking Blues is accompanied by a signed print.
Tyler Mitchell: Wish This Was Real, Collectors’ Edition

links.text: Tyler Mitchell: Wish This Was Real, Collectors’ Edition

blocks.text: Wish This Was Real is the definitive early-career survey by one of the most acclaimed photographic artists working today. Since his rise to prominence in the worlds of art and fashion Tyler Mitchell has created images of beauty, utopia, and the American landscape that expand the imaginary of Blackness in the twenty-first century. Offering new perspectives by leading writers on his long-standing themes of self-determination and the extraordinary radiance of the everyday, Wish This Was Real shows how photography can be rooted in a collective past while evoking imagined futures. This special collectors’ edition features three custom metallic-covered volumes alongside two posters, all enclosed in a deluxe folder and signed and numbered by the artist.
Deana Lawson: An Aperture Monograph, Limited Edition

links.text: Deana Lawson: An Aperture Monograph, Limited Edition

blocks.text: Deana Lawson portrays the personal and the powerful through her large-scale, dramatic portraits of people in the US, the Caribbean, and Africa. Lawson’s Aperture Monograph is the first photobook by the visionary artist, and this limited edition features a special slipcase, rose gold-gilded pages, and a custom tipped-on C-print on the cover. “Outside a Lawson portrait you might be working three jobs, just keeping your head above water, struggling,” writes Zadie Smith in her essay for the book. “But inside her frame you are beautiful, imperious, unbroken, unfallen.”
Dionne Lee: Currents, Book and Print Set

links.text: Dionne Lee: Currents, Book and Print Set

blocks.text: Dionne Lee works across photography, video, and collage to examine histories of land, power, survival, and Black identity in the American landscape. Using formal interventions and innovative darkroom techniques—including rephotographing found imagery from wilderness survival manuals and using graphite pencils to create inscriptions on her photographs of the landscape—Lee’s work is a powerful meditation on the land as a site of refuge and loss. Currents , the artist’s first monograph, brings together work from over a decade, offering a deeper look at a visionary artist reshaping how we see­—and choose to imagine—the great outdoors. For this set, the accompanying gelatin-silver print of a singular, meditative moment from her video Currents II (2024) was meticulously printed by the artist herself.
